sections.body:
Sleep is not nothing at all. Sleep is when your body does its busiest work of the day.

Your body is always busy. It keeps your heart beating, your lungs breathing, and your brain thinking. But some jobs cannot be done while you are awake and moving around. They need you to be still.

When you sleep, your body repairs itself. It fixes small wear and tear in your muscles and grows. That is why children, who are growing fast, need more sleep than grown-ups.

Your brain also does its tidying at night. During the day you learn things: new words, new facts, how to ride a bike. At night your brain sorts them, files them away, and keeps the useful ones. That is why a good night's sleep helps you remember the morning after.

Sleep also runs your daily clock. Your body has a rhythm that repeats about every 24 hours. That rhythm tells you when to feel awake and when to feel sleepy. It is called your body clock, or circadian rhythm.

Children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Grown-ups need less. If you miss sleep, you do not fall over. But you get clumsy, bad-tempered, and slow to learn.
examples: Sleep is not wasted time. It is when the body works.
Children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep.
I slept well, so I remembered everything today.
sections.heading: What sleep is, and why you need it

sections.body:
Sleep comes in turns. You drift in and out of deep sleep all night.

In **deep sleep** your body does its repair work. Your muscles let go of the tension you carried during the day. Your tissues mend. Growth hormone, the stuff that helps you grow, is released most in the deep part of the night. That is why a growth spurt often follows a good night.

Your heart slows down a little and your breathing becomes deep and regular. Your body temperature drops slightly. This is the quiet time.

After a deep stretch, you spend a while in **light sleep**. Your body rests, but your brain is more active. Then you move into the part of the night where **dreaming** happens. Your eyes move under their lids, even though you cannot see anything. Your brain is busy sorting and playing with the day you had.

Then you come up, turn over, and go down again. You cannot remember most of this, and that is normal. A good night is a short cycle, about 90 minutes, repeated several times.
examples: Deep sleep is when my muscles let go of the day's tiredness.
I grew a bit while I was sleeping.
Most nights I wake up without remembering my dreams.
sections.heading: What your body does while you sleep

sections.body:
Your brain has a lot to do overnight, and it does it in a careful order.

First it sorts. Everything you saw, heard and did during the day gets sorted into what matters and what does not. New skills get moved from short-term memory into long-term memory.

Then it practises. When you learn to ride a bike, the part of your brain that steers gets repeated again and again during sleep, without you knowing. That is why you sometimes wake up able to do something you could not do last night.

Sleep also cools your mind. The chemical that makes you alert stays high all day. During sleep it drops, so you can think clearly and feel calm again. When you do not sleep enough, that chemical stays high, and you feel nervous and cannot concentrate.

That is why a good night's sleep makes a hard day easier. Your brain needs sleep to put things in order. When you skip it, everything stays a bit jumbled.
examples: My brain sorts out the day while I am asleep.
I practised riding my bike in my sleep.
I slept badly, so I could not concentrate at all.
sections.heading: What your brain does while you sleep

sections.body:
A tired brain is a dangerous one. When people are sleepy, they react more slowly and they judge distance badly. That is why driving when tired can kill, and it is why adults stop for a rest when they feel drowsy.

A child who does not sleep enough often gets clumsy, falls more, and finds school harder. Sleep loss also makes people more likely to feel hungry, and to reach for sugary food.

Two habits make sleep harder. Bright screens in the evening tell your brain it is still daytime. And caffeine in tea, cola and energy drinks stays in your body for hours, long after you feel awake again. Both of these push your body clock later, so you fall asleep later and wake up more tired.
sections.heading: When too little sleep gets dangerous

sections.body:
These are the words you need to talk about sleep.

REM sleep is the part of the night when you dream most. Your brain is busy and your eyes move, but your body is still.

Your **body clock**, also called your circadian rhythm, is the daily rhythm inside you. It tells you when to be awake and when to be sleepy, and it follows the light and dark.

A **dream** is the story your brain makes while you sleep. Some people remember their dreams. Most do not.

Melatonin is the chemical your body makes in the evening to tell you it is time for bed. It rises when the light fades.
examples: REM sleep is when I dream the most.
My body clock follows the light.
Melatonin tells my body it is time for bed.
sections.heading: The words we use for sleep

terms.example: REM sleep gets longer as the night goes on.
terms.gloss: The part of the night when you dream most. Your brain is busy, but your body stays still.

terms.example: My body clock wakes me up before the alarm.
terms.gloss: The daily rhythm inside you that tells you when to be awake and when to be sleepy.

terms.example: I had a strange dream about a talking bicycle.
terms.gloss: The story your brain makes while you sleep. Some people remember them, most do not.

terms.example: Melatonin rises when the sun goes down.
terms.gloss: The chemical your body makes in the evening when the light fades, to tell you it is time for bed.

sections.body:
Good sleep is mostly a habit. Your body likes the same order every evening, and it likes the same times.

Start with the same bedtime, even at the weekend. A body clock learns a rhythm faster when you keep it.

Move the last hour of the day away from screens. A phone or a game is interesting, and the light on the screen tells your brain it is still daytime.
examples: I put my phone away an hour before bed.
We read a book instead of watching a screen.
I went to bed at the same time as last night.
sections.heading: How to build a bedtime that works
steps: Keep the same bedtime, even at the weekend.
Stop screens one hour before bed.
Do the same calm things each evening, like reading.
Keep your room dark, cool and quiet.
Get bright light and movement early in the day.

item.summary: Sleep is not wasted time. While you sleep your body repairs itself, your brain sorts what you learned, and your body clock resets for the next day. After reading this you can explain what sleep is for, say how many hours children need, name what happens to your body and brain at night, and build a bedtime routine that works.
item.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
